On this page

Toroidal inclusions ​

Before this page

Concentration and contribution tensors, for the tensors computed here, Elasticity and transport: one set of formulas, for the convention under which the conduction problem is written, and, in the documentation of TensND, Toroidal coordinates and Toroidal functions, for the coordinates and the functions in which the problem is written.

The inclusions of the previous chapters are ellipsoids, or patterns bounded by ellipsoids. This chapter treats two shapes that are not, and whose response to a remote loading is still known exactly. A torus is not an ellipsoid: the field inside a toroidal heterogeneity is not uniform and there is no Hill tensor. Its response to a remote loading is nonetheless known as a series, the torus being a coordinate surface of the toroidal system. This page solves the conduction problem of an insulating torus in an isotropic matrix and derives its concentration tensor. The problem was solved by Radi and Sevostianov with the same family of functions; the derivation is written here in the notation of the package, and the syntax is given in Toroidal inclusions.

1. The problem ​

A torus of axis , of center-line radius and of tube radius  , is embedded in an unbounded matrix of conductivity . No flux crosses its surface. Far from it the temperature gradient is uniform, equal to :

with the unit normal of the torus, outward. The mean gradient over the pore is defined from the values of the temperature on its surface, and is linear in :

is the gradient concentration tensor of the pore. Its flux concentration vanishes, so that the two contributions per unit volume of the torus are     and  . By symmetry about the axis,

and the two scalars depend on the ratio only: they are obtained from a gradient along the axis and from a gradient across it.

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization, TensND
TI = MeanFieldHomogenization.ToroidalInclusions
α₀ = acosh(2.0)
sh, ch, N, c = sinh(α₀), cosh(α₀), TI._series_length(α₀), 4 * sqrt(2) / π

b = TI._neumann_amplitudes(Val(:sine), 0, [c * n for n in 0:(N + 1)], α₀)
P, Q¹ = toroidal_P(N, 0, α₀), toroidal_Q(N, 1, α₀)
far = c * sh^3 / ch * sum(n * b[n] for n in 1:N)
surface = 1 - 8 * sqrt(2) / (3π) * sh^4 / ch * sum(n * b[n] * P[n + 1] * Q¹[n + 1] for n in 1:N)
(far, surface)
(2.0639074506992983, 2.063907450699297)
julia
b = TI._neumann_amplitudes(Val(:cosine), 1, [-(n == 0 ? c / 2 : c) for n in 0:(N + 1)], α₀)
P¹, Q¹, dQ¹ = toroidal_P(N, 1, α₀), toroidal_Q(N, 1, α₀), toroidal_dQ(N, 1, α₀)
far = c / 2 * sh^3 / ch * sum((n^2 - 1 / 4) * b[n + 1] for n in 0:N)
surface = 1 + 2 * sqrt(2) / (3π) * sh^4 / ch * sum(b[n + 1] * P¹[n + 1] * (2 * dQ¹[n + 1] + ch / sh * Q¹[n + 1]) for n in 0:N)
(far, surface)
(1.3996840651707634, 1.399684065170763)

Radi and Sevostianov write the perturbation with the amplitudes     along the axis and      across it. Their closed form of the (their equations 3.17 and 3.18) and their elimination for the (4.9 to 4.11) return the amplitudes computed here, and their integrals over the torus (5.5 and 5.8) are those above. The two expressions of this section are the values of these integrals; they stand for the expressions printed as (5.6) and (5.9) in the article, which differ from them.

8. Values ​

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization, TensND
using Plots

components(λ) = canonical_components(gradient_gradient_concentration(InsulatingTorus(1.0, λ), TensISO{3}(0.0), TensISO{3}(1.0)))[[1, 9]]
λs = range(0.01, 0.99; length = 99)
A = components.(λs)
plot(λs, [first.(A) last.(A)]; label = ["Aₜ (across the axis)" "Aₙ (along the axis)"],
    xlabel = "r / R", ylabel = "component of A", ylims = (1.2, 2.2),
    title = "Insulating torus: gradient concentration tensor", titlefontsize = 10, size = (640, 360))

A thin ring is, locally, a straight wire. A wire across the gradient has the concentration 2 of an insulating circular cylinder, and a wire along it does not disturb the field, with the concentration 1. A gradient along the axis is across the wire all around the ring, and a gradient across the axis is across the wire for half of it on average:

julia
components(1.0e-4)
2-element Vector{Float64}:
 1.4999999507311785
 2.0000000238494557

When the hole closes,  , both stay finite:

julia
components(0.99)
2-element Vector{Float64}:
 1.360007334347981
 2.0348449923737286

For comparison, the insulating sphere has   in every direction.

9. Scope ​

The series solves the problem in an isotropic matrix, for a torus of circular cross-section that conducts nothing. The number of terms is set by the value of : the radii are numbers or dual numbers, and the derivatives with respect to them go through the solve. InsulatingTorus is the inclusion; Toroidal inclusions shows its use, and Ring-shaped pores in a conducting matrix compares it with published values and with spheroids of the same volume.

Where to go next ​

The next page, Holes given by a conformal map, treats the other shape of this chapter: a cylindrical cavity of non-elliptic section, in elasticity and in conduction. The schemes take the torus through its concentration tensor, as they take any inclusion (Homogenization schemes).
